Hatzipolakis Triangle

GeometryTrianglesCircles
Game: Move the corners of a triangle and discover three lines where the marked dots always line up.
How to play: Drag A, B or C, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Press Check the claims to show and confirm the lines; the other buttons show extra marks.
Look for the math

Drop perpendiculars from one corner of a triangle onto the two angle bisectors from the other corners. Their feet join the side midpoints in one straight line, and each foot also sits on a line through two places where the incircle touches the sides. Drag the corners and the three lines survive every change of shape.

The first line: a right triangle's centre

Let M be the foot from A to the bisector at B. The triangle ABM is a right triangle, so its circumcenter is the midpoint F of the hypotenuse AB. Hence FM = AF = BF = AB/2. Isosceles triangle BFM gives angle AFM = angle ABC, so FM runs parallel to BC. A line through the midpoint F parallel to BC is the midline, and it passes through the other midpoint E. Thus M lies on EF; the same argument at C puts N there too.

Equal tangent lengths locate the other lines

The incircle centred at the incenter I touches BC at X, CA at Y and AB at Z. Tangents from one vertex have equal lengths: AY = AZ, BX = BZ, CX = CY. Together with EM = FM - EF = AB/2 - BC/2 this gives EM = EY, and the equal angles at E force X, Y, M onto one line. The mirror argument gives FN = FZ and the line X, Z, N.

What the page's subtraction really says

The chain on the original page writes EM = (AB - BC)/2 = EY. That is a signed difference: if AB is shorter than BC it is negative, while a length cannot be. The true length statement is EM = EY = |AB - BC|/2, and the logic test confirms it on thousands of triangles. In the same vein the page's step angle XCE = angle CEM is an equality of angles between lines: as angles between rays the two can be supplementary, yet X, Y, M stay straight. Cabart's shorter proof reflects A in the bisector at B onto BC; M is the midpoint of that segment, and Menelaus' theorem finishes the job. He calls that reflected point D, although the page already used D for the midpoint of BC — a harmless clash of letters.

How far the check goes

The logic test transcribes the applet a second way: its incenter is found by rotating two sides through half their angles and intersecting the bisectors, its touch points by the applet's projection formula, and its inradius by averaging the three distances from I. Those points agree with the port over hundreds of configurations. Both numbered claims and every step above were checked on thousands of randomly chosen triangles with sides of at least 2 units, the applet's own cut-off. No counterexample appeared; the only corrections were the absolute value and the reading of the angles as line angles.

Try dragging B past C so AB becomes shorter than BC: the three lines stay straight even though the page's subtraction turns negative.
